entities.name: Maximianus of Ravenna
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Maximianus (c. 499 – February 24, 556), a Dalmatian presbyter, ascended to the archepiscopal see of Ravenna in 546 CE, a strategic appointment by Emperor Justinian I amidst the Byzantine reconquest of Italy. His tenure as the first archbishop of Ravenna, succeeding a line of bishops, marked a critical period for the city as the de facto capital of Byzantine Italy, transforming it into a vibrant center of imperial power and Orthodox Christianity in the West. Maximianus's influence extended beyond ecclesiastical matters, encompassing significant secular administrative and political functions, effectively serving as Justinian's chief agent in the newly re-established Italian prefecture.

During his episcopacy, Maximianus was a prodigious patron of the arts, commissioning some of the most iconic mosaics of late antiquity. He oversaw the completion and consecration of the Basilica of San Vitale in 547 CE, where his own famous portrait mosaic appears alongside Emperor Justinian and Empress Theodora. He also initiated the construction of the Basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe and dedicated it in 549 CE. Beyond his architectural patronage, Maximianus played a crucial role in theological disputes, steadfastly supporting Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters, a contentious policy that alienated much of the Western episcopate, including the Bishop of Rome.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Maximianus's role as the first archbishop of Byzantine Ravenna solidified imperial control and promoted a distinct artistic and theological identity in Italy, leaving an indelible mark on Early Christian art and the city's historical trajectory. His patronage of monumental mosaics and architecture profoundly shaped Ravenna's cultural landscape, making it a key site for studying Byzantine influence in the West.
